title: The Forbidden City
objective: After this level you can describe Beijing's palace city.
summary: Begun 1406, occupied 1420, barred to most subjects. Buildings are ranked on a south-facing axis, and the halls are timber post-and-lintel frames. A museum since 1925.

cards.headline: For five centuries, most people were barred from China's palace.
cards.body: That's the Forbidden City's name explained: access was barred to most of the realm's subjects. The Yongle emperor of the Ming dynasty commissioned it in 1406, and the court moved in in 1420. So what was behind the wall?

cards.headline: A city where everything lines up
cards.body: Just what Level 33 described: not one building but many, behind a high wall and a moat about 52 metres wide. Inside, the most important buildings stand on a north-south axis and face south, to honour the Sun. The Palace Museum says every structure followed the traditional architectural hierarchy, designed to reflect imperial power. Here, where a building stood told you how much it mattered.

mascot.line: Face south, line up, know your rank. Even the buildings had manners.

cards.headline: Up the terraces to the throne
cards.body: In the Outer Court, three main halls of government stand on a three-tiered marble terrace above an immense plaza. The grandest is the Hall of Supreme Harmony, home of the emperor's throne and the largest single building in the compound. Behind the Outer Court, the Inner Court held the imperial living quarters. Government at the front, family at the back.

cards.fact: The emperor's palace uses Level 3's oldest trick.
cards.context: Its halls are timber buildings with post-and-lintel frames under tiled roofs: posts holding up beams, like Stonehenge. The Forbidden City stayed the centre of Chinese power for five centuries. Puyi, the last Qing emperor, left in 1924, and in 1925 the Palace Museum was established there. Forbidden no longer.

cards.headline: The Forbidden City: entered
learned: Commissioned 1406; the court moved in in 1420
Buildings ranked on a south-facing axis
Timber post-and-lintel halls; a museum since 1925

questions.prompt: Why is Beijing's imperial palace called the Forbidden City?

options.label: It was built on land where building had been forbidden
options.rationale: The name is about who could enter.

options.label: Access was barred to most of the realm's subjects
The Ming banned anyone from painting it
Its moat was forbidden to boats
options.rationale: The whole city was closed to most subjects.

questions.explanation: It was so named because access was barred to most of the subjects of the realm.

questions.prompt: Which way do the Forbidden City's most important buildings face, and why?

options.label: North, toward the old border walls
East, toward the sunrise over the sea
Toward the moat, to watch for attackers
options.rationale: Their facing honours the Sun, not the moat.

questions.explanation: The most important buildings, especially those on the north-south axis, face south to honour the Sun.

questions.prompt: The Forbidden City's timber halls share a structural system with Level 3's Stonehenge. What is it?

options.label: A steel skeleton carrying every floor
Domes raised ring by ring with no frame

questions.explanation: Its buildings use timber post-and-lintel frames: upright posts holding up horizontal beams, the system Stonehenge is built on.
